Millard Fillmore: President of the United States from 1850 to 1853.
Born in Mecca to the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh, this Arab leader is regarded in Islam as the final prophet, the Seal of the Prophets — who is he?

Born into a Lahore industrial family and the longest-serving prime minister in Pakistan's history — across three non-consecutive terms, each one ending in his ousting — who is this politician and businessman?
Nawaz Sharif: Prime Minister of Pakistan (1990–1993; 1997–1999; 2013–2017)

A communist Eastern Bloc state founded in 1945, it launched a successful 1975 offensive against its southern rival before merging the next year into a single Socialist Republic — what was this country?
North Vietnam: Country in Southeast Asia (1945–1976)
Once Britain's youngest sitting MP — who crossed from Conservative to independent to Labour — this baronet then founded the British Union of Fascists in 1932. Who was he?
The first Carolingian to hold the Frankish throne, this son of Charles Martel began his reign in 751 after years as joint Mayor of the Palace with his brother — who was he?
Pepin the Short: King of the Franks from 751 to 768.
This ancient Indian king fought valiantly against Alexander the Great at the Battle of the Hydaspes in 326 BC, and was rewarded with an expanded realm despite his defeat — who is he?
A chartered accountant turned politician, this Rajya Sabha member spent years as an outspoken Aam Aadmi Party figure before defecting to the BJP in April 2026 — who is he?
Born in 1994, this German politician led the Green Youth, then served as her party's women's-policy spokeswoman before becoming co-leader of the Greens in 2022 — who is she?
Ricarda Lang: German politician (born 1994). Ricarda Lang (born 17 January 1994) is a German politician of the Alliance 90/The Greens who has been serving as a member of the Bundestag since 2021.
Produced annually by WWE since 1988, this event's signature match sees wrestlers enter the ring one at a time on a timer rather than all at once — what's the event?
Royal Rumble: World Wrestling Entertainment event series.
This French explorer crossed the Atlantic some two dozen times, drew the first accurate maps of North America's eastern coast and Great Lakes, and founded Quebec City in 1608. Who was he?
Samuel de Champlain: French explorer of North America (1574–1635)
Known until 2003 as the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, this Balkan union dissolved in 2006 when its junior partner voted for independence — which two-republic state?
Serbia and Montenegro: Country in Southeast Europe (1992–2006)

Defended by weapons designed by the polymath Archimedes, this Roman conquest of a Sicilian city in 213–212 BC ended with the inventor's death at a soldier's hands despite orders to spare him — which historic clash?
Siege of Syracuse (213–212 BC): Roman victory during the Second Punic War.

This doctrine holding that governing authority is legitimate to some degree — especially over taxation and production — gained traction in American political discourse during the 1930s and '40s, its opposite being anarchism — what's it called?

Statism: Doctrine that the political authority of the state is legitimate to some degree. In political science, statism or etatism (from French, état 'state') is the doctrine that the political authority of the state is legitimate to some degree.
Serving as Ottoman Grand Vizier during World War I, this convicted war criminal is remembered as the architect of the Armenian genocide — who was he?

A protégé of Robert Walpole, this Whig statesman served as a Secretary of State for 30 unbroken years and dominated British foreign policy — and was twice Prime Minister. By which dukedom is he commonly known?
Thomas Pelham-Holles, 1st Duke of Newcastle: Prime Minister of Great Britain (1754–1756; 1757–1762)
This Norse god sacrificed his right hand to bind the monstrous wolf Fenrir, and English weekdays still preserve his name in the middle of the work week — who is he?

Spanning roughly 800 to 1050 CE, this era of Norse raiding, trading, and settlement saw Scandinavians reach as far as Newfoundland, becoming the first Europeans known to set foot in North America. What period was this?
Viking Age: Period of European history (about 800–1050)
Fought from December 1812 to May 1814, this multinational alliance of European powers finally defeated Napoleon's empire and forced him into exile on Elba — which conflict?
War of the Sixth Coalition: 1813–1814 conflict during the Napoleonic Wars.
Commander of the Indonesian Armed Forces during the country's 1998 transition from authoritarian rule, this retired general later chaired the Presidential Advisory Council — who is it?
Wiranto: Indonesian general and politician. On 27 July 2016, Wiranto was appointed Coordinating Minister for Political, Legal, and Security Affairs, replacing Luhut Binsar Panjaitan.
A graduate of Cairo University who briefly served as Japan's defense minister in 2007, this politician has governed Tokyo since 2016 — who is she?
Yuriko Koike: Governor of Tokyo since 2016. Yuriko Koike (Japanese: 小池 百合子, Hepburn: Koike Yuriko; born 15 July 1952) is a Japanese politician who has served as the Governor of Tokyo since 2016.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Zhuge Liang (born 181) is the earliest of the four. After helping found Shu Han, Zhuge Liang exercised near-total authority over both civil and military affairs.
Which of these people was born first?
Levi Strauss (born 1829) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was born first?
Jan Hus (born 1369) is the earliest of the four. Hus is considered to be the first Church reformer, even though some designate the theorist John Wycliffe.
Pascal (programming language) (founded 1970) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is an astronomer?
Annie S. D. Maunder is an astronomer. As sole author, she also devised with her husband, Edward Walter Maunder, the butterfly diagram for sunspots.
Pick the mathematician from these four.

William James Sidis is a mathematician. Born to Boris Sidis, a prominent psychiatrist, and Sarah Mandelbaum Sidis, a physician, Sidis demonstrated extraordinary intellectual capabilities from infancy.
What is the atomic number of Tellurium?
Tellurium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Te and atomic number 52.
What is the atomic number of Manganese?
Manganese is a chemical element; it has the symbol Mn and atomic number 25.
In what year was David Attenborough born?
David Attenborough: Sir David Frederick Attenborough ( AT-ən-bər-ə; born 8 May 1926) is an English broadcaster, natural historian, and writer.
In what year was Eratosthenes born?
Eratosthenes eventually became the chief librarian at the Library of Alexandria.
In what year was Michael Faraday born?
Michael Faraday: Although Faraday received little formal education, as a self-made man, he was one of the most influential scientists in history.
In what year did Carlo Acutis die?
Carlo Acutis: Acutis was canonised on 7 September 2025, alongside Pier Giorgio Frassati.
In what year did Srinivasa Ramanujan die?
Srinivasa Ramanujan Iyengar (22 December 1887 – 26 April 1920) was an Indian mathematician who worked during the early 20th century.
In what year was Uncertainty principle discovered?
Uncertainty principle: The uncertainty principle, also known as Heisenberg's indeterminacy principle, is a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics.

Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. Approximately 60 countries across four continents have flown the MiG-21, and it still serves many nations seven decades after its maiden flight.
Zinc: Pfizer. Zinc is a chemical element; it has symbol Zn and atomic number 30.
In which country is Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker?
Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker: United States. It has a narrower fuselage and is shorter than the 707.
Who is credited with discovering Roentgenium?
GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
Roentgenium: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research. Roentgenium (German: [ʁœntˈɡeːni̯ʊm]) is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Rg and atomic number 111.
Who is credited with discovering 4 Vesta?
4 Vesta: Heinrich Wilhelm Olbers. Vesta (minor-planet designation: 4 Vesta) is one of the largest objects in the asteroid belt, with a mean diameter of 525 kilometres (326 mi).
Who is credited with discovering Lysosome?
Lysosome: Christian de Duve. A lysosome (/ˈlaɪsəˌsoʊm/) is a membrane-bound organelle that is found in all animal cells (except red blood cells), and rarely in plant cells.
People with this anxiety disorder dread places they feel they can't escape — crowds, queues, public transit — and in severe cases may become unable to leave home at all. What is it?
Agoraphobia is an anxiety disorder characterized by symptoms of anxiety in situations where the person perceives their environment to be unsafe with no way to escape.
Found on every continent but Antarctica and almost always monogamous breeders, which bird family unites ducks, geese, and swans under one scientific name?
Anatidae are the biological family of water birds that includes ducks, geese, and swans.

Once classified as bacteria and originally called archaebacteria, this domain of mostly single-celled prokaryotic organisms turns out to be the ancestral lineage from which eukaryotes evolved — which domain of life?
Archaea (ar-KEE-) is a domain of organisms.
One of the first grains ever domesticated, this cereal crop was cultivated in the Fertile Crescent around 9000 BC and later spread throughout Eurasia by 2000 BC — name the grain?
Barley (Hordeum vulgare), a member of the grass family, is a major cereal grain grown in temperate climates globally.
Represented most commonly as a 1 or a 0, this portmanteau of 'binary digit' is the most fundamental unit of information in computing — what is it called?
Bit is the most basic unit of information in computing and digital communication.
One of only two elements liquid at room temperature, this reddish-brown, pungent-smelling element takes its name from the Greek word for 'stench.' What element is it (symbol Br)?
Bromine is a chemical element; it has symbol Br and atomic number 35.
Native to nearly all of South America, this semiaquatic, grass-munching cousin of the guinea pig holds the title of largest living rodent — what is it?
Capybara (Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris) is the largest living rodent, native to all countries in South America except Chile.
Known as garbanzo, chana or Bengal gram, this protein-rich legume is mashed into hummus and fried into falafel, with its oldest remains found in Syria — what is it?
Chickpea (Cicer arietinum) is an annual legume of the family Fabaceae, subfamily Faboideae, cultivated for its edible seeds.
Found naturally in the sap of the opium poppy and a prodrug of morphine, which opiate treats mild-to-moderate pain and is often paired with paracetamol?
Codeine is an opiate and prodrug of morphine mainly used to treat pain, coughing, and diarrhea.

Derived from an Ancient Greek word for 'flesh,' this breakdown product of muscle and protein metabolism is released into the bloodstream at a rate depending on a person's muscle mass — name the substance?
Creatinine (from Ancient Greek (kras) 'flesh') is a breakdown product of creatine phosphate from muscle and protein metabolism.
A colorless, volatile liquid (CH2Cl2) with a sweet, chloroform-like odor, it's slightly polar, mixes with many organic solvents but not water, and is widely used as a solvent — what is it?
Dichloromethane (DCM, methylene chloride, or methylene bichloride) is an organochlorine compound with the formula CH2Cl2.
This English physician created the world's first vaccine, targeting smallpox, and in doing so coined the very term 'vaccine' — derived from the Latin for 'pustules of the cow.' Who was he?
Edward Jenner (17 May 1749 - 26 January 1823) was an English physician and scientist who pioneered the concept of vaccines and created the smallpox vaccine, the world's first vaccine.
This flowering plant in the family Erythroxylaceae is one of just two species cultivated for their alkaloid-rich leaves — what is its scientific name?
Erythroxylum coca is a species of flowering plant in the family Erythroxylaceae.

Species in the stinging genus Solenopsis are sometimes confused with unrelated weaver insects in Southeast Asia that share their reddish color and painful bite — what's the common name for this group?
Fire ant are several species of ants in the genus Solenopsis, which includes over 200 species.
Caused by abnormalities in the genome, this category of health problem may arise from a single faulty gene, many genes, or a chromosome abnormality — what is the general term?
Genetic disorder is a health problem caused by one or more abnormalities in the genome.
Designed in the late 1950s as a replacement for the piston-engined E-1 Tracer, this twin-turboprop U.S. Navy aircraft provides carrier-based early warning radar coverage. Name the aircraft?
Grumman E-2 Hawkeye is an American all-weather, carrier-capable, tactical airborne early warning (AEW) aircraft.

Fox-sized and found on every continent but Australia and Antarctica, these primitive ornithischian dinosaurs are known for odd teeth — canine-like tusks plus cheek teeth built for chewing. What's this family?
Heterodontosauridae is a family of ornithischian dinosaurs that were likely among the most basal (primitive) members of the group.

Literally meaning 'below mania,' this psychiatric condition brings a non-contextual elevation of mood along with increased energy, irritability, and impulsivity, but without the psychotic features of full mania — name this condition?
Hypomania (literally "below mania" or "less than mania") is a psychiatric condition of abnormally heightened mood and increased energy that is less severe than mania.
Native to Africa and Eurasia, which group of opportunistic canid predators includes the black-backed, side-striped, and golden species?
Jackal are canids native to Africa and Eurasia.
This Columbia economist won the Nobel in 2001 and famously skewers his laissez-faire colleagues as "free-market fundamentalists" — who is he?
Joseph Stiglitz (born February 9, 1943) is an American New Keynesian economist, a public policy analyst, political activist, and a professor at Columbia University.
This American economist served as U.S. Treasury Secretary, later led the National Economic Council, and was the 27th president of Harvard before resigning a professorship there in 2026 — who is he?
Larry Summers (born November 30, 1954) is an American economist.
This Chinese computer engineer turned science-fiction writer won the 2015 Hugo Award for his novel The Three-Body Problem, and has also claimed China's Galaxy Award a record nine times. Who is he?
Liu Cixin (pinyin: Li Cxn,; born 23 June 1963) is a Chinese computer engineer and science fiction writer.

Living from about 6.2 million years ago until roughly 4,000 years ago, this extinct relative of modern elephants is distinguished by its large, spirally twisted tusks and cold-weather adaptations like a thick fur coat — name the animal?
Mammoth is a member of the extinct elephantid genus Mammuthus.
Home to a relativistic plasma jet stretching nearly 5,000 light-years from its core, this giant elliptical galaxy sits in the constellation Virgo — which galaxy is it?
Messier 87 (also known as Virgo A or NGC 4486, generally abbreviated to M87) is a supergiant elliptical galaxy in the constellation Virgo that contains several trillion stars.
This genus of edible sac fungi has a honeycomb-like cap of ridges and pits, is prized in French and Catalan cooking, and turns toxic if eaten raw or undercooked. What fungus is this?
Morchella is a genus of edible sac fungi closely related to anatomically simpler cup fungi in the order Pezizales (division Ascomycota).

First arising in wormlike creatures some 550 million years ago, this body-wide network coordinates actions and relays sensory signals through a central half and a peripheral half — what system is being described?
Nervous system is the highly complex part of an animal that coordinates its actions and sensory information by transmitting signals to and from different parts of its body.
Concerned with the most fundamental concept of all — being — this branch of metaphysics distinguishes non-repeatable particulars from repeatable universals like 'green' — what is the field?
Ontology is the philosophical study of being.
Named after a 17th-century French mathematician and physicist, this SI unit of pressure is defined as one newton of force per square metre — name the unit?
Pascal (unit) (symbol: Pa) is the unit of pressure in the International System of Units (SI).
Prized as an ornamental indoor plant and still poorly understood taxonomically, this arum-family genus ranks second in size only to Anthurium — which genus?
Philodendron is a large genus of flowering plants in the family Araceae.
This category of polymer includes both natural proteins like wool and silk, and synthetic materials like nylon and aramid fibers — what is it?
Polyamide is a polymer with repeating units linked by amide bonds.
This noncontagious autoimmune condition leaves dry, scaly patches of skin and can flare at the exact spot of an injury — a quirk called the Koebner phenomenon; what is it?
Psoriasis is a long-lasting, noncontagious autoimmune disease characterized by patches of abnormal skin.
What dimensionless quantity in fluid dynamics, expressing the ratio of inertial to viscous forces, determines whether a flow will be smooth and laminar or chaotic and turbulent?
Reynolds number (Re) is a dimensionless quantity that helps predict fluid flow patterns in different situations by measuring the ratio between inertial and viscous forces.
Named after an American veterinary surgeon, this genus of rod-shaped, gram-negative bacteria includes over 2,650 serotypes within a single major species — name it?
Salmonella is a genus of rod-shaped, (bacillus) Gram-negative bacteria of the family Enterobacteriaceae.
This Pakistani-American businessman owns both an NFL franchise, the Jacksonville Jaguars, and an English Premier League club, Fulham — who is he?
Shahid Khan (born July 18, 1950) is a Pakistani and American businessman.
The largest of the toothed whales and the largest toothed predator alive, this pelagic giant has females who give birth only every four to twenty years — what is it?
Sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus) is the largest of the toothed whales and the largest toothed predator.

Which British single-seat fighter plane, the only such aircraft Britain produced continuously throughout World War II, was famous for its innovative elliptical wing designed to be as thin as possible?
Supermarine Spitfire is a British single-seat fighter aircraft that was used by the Royal Air Force and other Allied countries before, during, and after World War II.
Used to treat asthma and COPD, this methylxanthine drug — a cousin of caffeine — turns up in trace amounts in tea, chocolate, and yerba mate. What is it?
Theophylline is a drug that inhibits phosphodiesterase and blocks adenosine receptors.
Formed from glycerol bonded to three fatty acids, these molecules make up the main constituents of body fat in humans and are also major components of human skin oil — what are they?
Triglyceride (from tri- and glyceride; also TG, triacylglycerol, TAG, or triacylglyceride) is an ester derived from glycerol and three fatty acids.
Known also as sight or eyesight, this sense lets the body detect photons and build a picture of its environment using daytime or night modes — what is it?
Visual perception is the ability to detect light and use it to form an image of the surrounding environment.
Known for a rapid side-to-side flight just before landing and living only in colonies, these black-and-yellow social wasps of the genera Vespula and Dolichovespula go by what North American name?
Yellowjacket is the common name in North America for predatory social wasps of the genera Vespula and Dolichovespula.
A rapid rise-and-fall of voltage across a cell membrane, this "spike" depolarizes neighboring spots and is how neurons and muscle cells fire — what is this electrical event called?
Action potential: Neuron communication by electric impulses.
Beginning about six hours after someone dependent on drinking stops, this set of symptoms can include shaking, sweating, seizures, and life-threatening delirium -- what is it called?
Formed when hydrogen atoms in ammonia are swapped out for carbon-based groups, which class of nitrogen-containing organic compounds includes aniline as its simplest aromatic member?
Amine: Chemical compounds and groups containing nitrogen with a lone pair (:N)

A German pharmacist coined this pigment's name from the Greek for 'flower' and 'dark blue' in 1835 — it shifts red to purple to blue depending on pH and colors blueberries, black rice, and autumn leaves; what is it?
Native to eastern North America's wet woods and swamps, this shrub genus produces bitter 'chokeberries' that reached Scandinavia and Russia by the eighteenth century — what genus is this?

Aronia: Genus of plants (chokeberries). Aronia is a genus of deciduous shrubs, the chokeberries, in the family Rosaceae native to eastern North America and most commonly found in wet woods and swamps.
Derived from a Greek word meaning 'that which is thought worthy,' which term denotes a statement accepted as true without proof, serving as a starting point for further reasoning?
Axiom: Statement that is taken to be true.
This common, noncancerous enlargement of a male gland can cause frequent urination and a weak stream; it isn't linked to poor hygiene, and there's no known cure. What's the condition?
Benign prostatic hyperplasia: Noncancerous increase in size of the prostate gland.
Composed of plasma plus red cells, white cells, and platelets, this circulatory fluid delivers oxygen and nutrients to the body while carrying away waste — what is it?
Blood: Body fluid in the circulatory system. Plasma, which constitutes 55% of blood fluid, is mostly water (92% by volume), and contains proteins, glucose, mineral ions, and hormones.
This plant family — nicknamed the mustards or crucifers, and including cabbage — hosts the caterpillars of a notorious garden-pest butterfly as one of its worst enemies — name the family?

Ranging from the hefty black species of the Amazon basin to the diminutive dwarf species just over a metre long, these Central and South American relatives of alligators make up their own reptile subfamily — what are they called?
Caiman: Subfamily of reptiles. The black caiman is the largest caiman species in the world and is found in the slow-moving rivers and lakes that surround the Amazon basin.

Born in London, raised in Milan, and self-taught in web design, this Catholic teenager built a website cataloguing Eucharistic miracles before dying of leukemia at fifteen — he was beatified in 2020. Who was he?
Which second-generation antihistamine for hay fever kicks in within half an hour but is more likely than fexofenadine or loratadine to cause drowsiness?

Cetirizine: Antihistamine medication. Cetirizine is a second-generation peripherally selective antihistamine used to treat allergic rhinitis (hay fever), dermatitis, urticaria (hives), and runny nose.
This plant genus includes both chicory, whose roasted roots make a coffee substitute, and true endive, the base for salad greens like escarole — which genus?
Cichorium: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family Asteraceae.

Believed to be the first coffee species ever cultivated, this plant, native to the forests of Ethiopia, South Sudan, and Yemen, still accounts for roughly 60% of global coffee production — what's its scientific name?
Coffea arabica: Species of coffee plant. Coffea arabica, also known as the Arabica coffee, is a species of flowering plant in the coffee and madder family Rubiaceae.
Found only in placental mammals, this roughly four-inch bundle of 200 to 300 million nerve fibers is the brain's largest white-matter structure, linking its left and right hemispheres — what is it?
Corpus callosum: White matter tract connecting the two cerebral hemispheres.
Inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, this disorder coats the lungs and other organs in thick mucus, inviting repeated bacterial infections — what genetic condition is it?
Cystic fibrosis: Genetic disorder affecting mostly the lungs.

Doctors once spotted this endocrine condition by its three Ps — polydipsia, polyuria, and polyphagia, or excessive thirst, urination, and hunger — all tracing back to trouble with insulin. Which disease is it?
Diabetes: Group of endocrine diseases characterized by high blood sugar levels.

Aristotle's Poetics contrasted this performance-based mode with the epic and the lyrical, and its name comes from a Greek word meaning "deed" or "act" — the two-masks symbol marks its split into comedy and tragedy. What is it?
Drama: Artwork intended for performance; formal type of literature.
Named for the large trunk-like proboscis of its males, this giant oceangoing pinniped can weigh up to 4,000 kilograms and was once hunted nearly to extinction for lamp oil. What animal is it?
Elephant seal: Genus of aquatic carnivores.
Sold under the brand name Nexium, this proton pump inhibitor treats acid reflux by blocking an enzyme in the stomach's acid-producing cells — what is it?
Esomeprazole: Medication which reduces stomach acid.
While its deciduous neighbors drop everything and go bare for winter, this kind of plant keeps its foliage green and working all year round — what's the botanical term?
Evergreen: Plant that has leaves in all seasons.
This beetle family produces light mainly at twilight to attract mates — though some females mimic another species' flash pattern just to lure and eat the males — what are they commonly called?
Firefly: Family of beetles. The Lampyridae are a family of elateroid beetles with more than 2,400 described species, many of which are light-emitting.
A French economist who gave up accounting to lecture across France, he founded peace societies and the Inter-Parliamentary Union before sharing the very first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901. Who was he?
Frédéric Passy: French economist and pacifist (1822–1912)

Among the longest of all living crocodilians, this fish-eater wields a slender snout lined with 110 interlocking teeth, and the males sport a bulbous, pot-shaped bump on the tip that gives the animal its name. What is it?
Gharial: Crocodilian native to the Indian subcontinent.
The seeds of five plants in this family, including rice, wheat, maize, barley, and sugar cane, cover 46% of the world's farmland — what group of plants is this?
Grass: Collective name for three families of plants.
This British mathematician has studied the math of dating and pandemics, delivered the Royal Institution's 2019 Christmas Lectures, and hosted BBC's 'Secret Genius of Modern Life' — who is she?
Hannah Fry: British mathematician and broadcaster (born 1984)
Its name Greek for 'different wings,' this insect suborder of about 40,000 species is the group most consistently termed 'true bugs' within Hemiptera — which group is it?
Heteroptera: Suborder of true bugs. The name "Heteroptera" is used in two very different ways in modern classifications.
Also known as dihydrocodeinone, this semi-synthetic opioid is often combined with acetaminophen or ibuprofen for pain and is sold alone as an extended-release drug called Zohydro ER — what is it?
Hydrocodone: Opioid drug used in pain relief.
First described to Europeans in 1812, this reddish-brown African antelope's males sport lyre-shaped horns up to three feet long — which animal?
Impala: Species of antelope found in Africa.

This Scottish physicist's equations unified electricity, magnetism, and light into a single theory — the second great unification in physics after Newton's — while also helping found statistical mechanics — who is he?
James Clerk Maxwell: Scottish physicist and mathematician (1831–1879)
Nicknamed 'Father of the National Parks,' this Scottish-born naturalist co-founded the Sierra Club and helped preserve Yosemite Valley and Sequoia National Park — who is he?
Nicknamed the 'honey bear' though unrelated to actual bears, this nocturnal rainforest mammal is the only member of its genus and a cousin of raccoons and coatis — which arboreal creature?
This biennial vegetable in the onion family has an edible bundle of leaf sheaths sometimes colloquially called a 'stem' — what is it?
Leek: Vegetable in the onion family. A leek is a biennial vegetable, a cultivar of Allium ampeloprasum, the broadleaf wild leek (syn.
Tucked mostly beneath the right rib cage, this organ detoxifies the body, stores glucose as glycogen, and produces the bile that helps digest fat — which organ?
Liver: Vertebrate organ involved in metabolism.
First synthesized in 1912 by a Merck chemist, this stimulant known on the street as ecstasy or molly became linked to raves and electronic dance music in the 1980s — which drug?
MDMA: Psychoactive drug, often called ecstasy.
Known by the pseudonym 'Notch,' this Swedish programmer created the best-selling video game of all time and became a billionaire when Microsoft bought his studio for $2.5 billion in 2014 — who is he?
Markus Persson: Swedish video game programmer (born 1979)
This rose-family shrub, commonly known as the medlar, produces fruit that's traditionally eaten only after it has softened past ripeness — what's its scientific name?
Mespilus germanica: Fruit tree, the medlar. Mespilus germanica, known as the medlar or common medlar, is a large shrub or small tree in the rose family Rosaceae.
Produced by mammary glands and rich in calcium, protein and lactose, this liquid is often prized for its antibody-packed early form, colostrum — what is it?
Milk: Nutrient-rich liquid produced by mammals.
Named for a Tanzanian teenager who studied it scientifically in the 1960s, this puzzling phenomenon claims hot liquids can sometimes freeze faster than cold ones — what is it called?
Mpemba effect: Natural phenomenon that hot water freezes faster than cold.

Nicknamed the 'flesh-eating disease' even though the bacteria don't actually consume tissue — they release toxins that kill it instead — this fast-spreading infection often enters through a cut or burn. What condition is it?
Necrotizing fasciitis: Infection that results in the death of the body's soft tissue.
This carnivorous freshwater fish, found widely across cold waters worldwide, has a current all-tackle world record of 25 kg, caught in Germany in 1986 — what species is it?
Northern pike: Species of fish. The northern pike (Esox lucius), also known as jack, northern or simply pike, is a species of carnivorous fish of the genus Esox (pikes).
A woody perennial native to the Mediterranean and a close relative of sweet marjoram, this mint-family herb is a staple of Italian and Greek cooking — what is it?
This term describes the bulk functional tissue of an organ like the brain or lungs, the filler tissue inside flatworms, and certain leaf cross-section layers in plants — what is it?
Parenchyma: Visceral tissue found inside organs of animals.
Discovered in 1972 and used to treat scabies and lice, this pyrethroid insecticide is safe for most mammals but especially dangerous to cats, who metabolize it slowly — what is it?
Permethrin: Medication and insecticide. It is applied to the skin as a cream or lotion.
Scientifically named Cajanus cajan, this perennial Fabaceae legume is a staple crop across the Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia, Africa, and the Caribbean — what is it?
Pigeon pea: Species of perennial legume. The pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan) is a perennial legume from the family Fabaceae native to the Eastern Hemisphere.
Though they look like dolphins, these small toothed whales are actually closer kin to narwhals and belugas, with flat spade-shaped teeth instead of dolphins' cone-shaped ones — what are they called?
Porpoise: Small cetacean of the family Phocoenidae.

Found in more than 200 species of mushroom, this tryptamine alkaloid is itself biologically inactive — the body must dephosphorylate it into psilocin before the euphoria and time-bending kick in. What is it?
Psilocybin: Chemical compound found in some species of mushrooms.
Flying aboard Soyuz T-11 in April 1984 as part of the Soviet Interkosmos programme, who became the first citizen of his country to reach outer space?
Rakesh Sharma: First Indian to travel to space (born 1949)
He shared the 1965 Nobel for quantum electrodynamics and dreamed up a now-famous pictorial shorthand for the behavior of subatomic particles — which physicist lent his name to those diagrams?
About 500 times sweeter than table sugar but prone to a bitter, metallic aftertaste, this odorless artificial sweetener also goes by the additive code E954 — what is it?

Native to the North Pacific coastline, this marine mammal is the heaviest member of the weasel family yet one of the smallest marine mammals, and one of few animals known to use rocks as tools to crack open shells — what is it?
Sea otter: Species of marine mammal. The sea otter (Enhydra lutris) is a marine mammal native to the coasts of the northern and eastern North Pacific Ocean.

No metal beats this one for electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity, or reflectivity, and it's mostly mined as a byproduct of refining copper, gold, lead, and zinc — which element, symbol Ag, is it?
